title: Etsy AI training terms change
content:
Etsy AI training terms change (2026)
Etsy & its "third party partners and vendors" will have the right to train artificial intelligence (AI) on what users upload to the online marketplace from December 16, 2026, under revised Terms of Use.[1][2] Etsy published those Terms & a new Privacy Policy on October 26, 2026;[1][2][3] the policy says Etsy may use content such as listing information, product reviews & community posts to train AI models.[4]
The clause is "subject to any applicable opt-out rights described in our Privacy Policy",[1] but marketplace news site Value Added Resource reported that neither the Terms nor the Privacy Policy names a general way specifically for US sellers to keep their listing photos, descriptions or other uploads out of AI training while they keep selling on Etsy.[2] The policy counts continued use after notice of its changes as acceptance & tells users who disagree that "you may close your account".[5]
AI training rights over user content
[edit | edit source]
Terms of Use clause
[edit | edit source]
Liz Morton, founder & editor of marketplace news site Value Added Resource, reported on October 29, 2026 that Etsy's updated Terms of Use were published on October 26 & will take effect on December 16, 2026.[2] The version of Etsy's Terms of Use marked "Last updated on Sep 30, 2026" describes itself as "a legally binding contract between you and Etsy".[6]
Value Added Resource wrote that the revised Terms add "explicit authorization for AI training and development".[2] The added sentence in the revised Terms reads:
This also includes the right for us and our third party partners and vendors to use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, including to improve the Services and/or help keep them safe, subject to any applicable opt-out rights described in our Privacy Policy.[1][2]
Privacy Policy language
[edit | edit source]
Etsy's new Privacy Policy states that it "was published on October 26, 2026, and will take effect on December 16, 2026".[3] Under the heading "Where necessary for our legitimate interests", the policy says Etsy "may also use Content you upload to our Services", such as listing information, product reviews & community posts, "to train and develop artificial intelligence and machine learning models", including for new features "like AI listing tools or AI review summaries".[4]
Etsy relies there on its own legitimate interests or those of third parties where they are "not outweighed by your rights and freedoms",[4] & the policy says that for users outside the European Economic Area (EEA), Switzerland or the United Kingdom (UK), "the legal bases on which we rely may differ".[3]
In a separate row of the same table, the policy says Etsy may also share uploaded Content, "e.g., listing information, product reviews, community posts", & other information it collects with its "fraud and security suppliers, to improve their services and our own", in order to keep its marketplace "safe and secure" & enforce its policies.[7]
License already in the Terms
[edit | edit source]
The Terms marked "Last updated on Sep 30, 2026" define "Your Content" as content a user posts using Etsy's services, such as shop names, listing photos, listing descriptions, reviews & videos, & say Etsy does not "make any claim to it".[6] Posting it grants Etsy &, "as authorized by Etsy in its sole discretion", third parties "a license to use it".[6] A subsection Etsy called "the legalese version of the last section" describes a "non-exclusive, worldwide, royalty-free, irrevocable, sub-licensable, perpetual" license "to use, display, edit, modify, reproduce, distribute, store, and prepare derivative works of Your Content".[6]
The examples Etsy gives in those Terms say it has permission to display a listing photo or video to buyers & can "resize or enhance it so it looks good to a buyer using our mobile app", can translate an English description "into French so a buyer in Paris can learn the story behind your item", & can feature a seller's photo or video "on our homepage, in one of our blogs or even on a billboard" to promote the seller's business & Etsy's.[6] Value Added Resource wrote that because the existing license was already broad enough to give Etsy extensive rights to use seller content, the new language "does not necessarily mean" Etsy is beginning AI training with that information "for the first time".[2]
Acceptance and opt-out
[edit | edit source]
Continued use as acceptance
[edit | edit source]
Etsy's new Privacy Policy says that a user who keeps using the Services after Etsy gives notice of changes, or after the user learns about them, is "accepting and agreeing to the updated Privacy Policy".[5] The policy adds: "If you do not agree with the changes, you may close your account."[5] Etsy's Terms of Use, last updated on September 30, 2026, say that use of the Services "after the effective date of the changes constitutes your acceptance of the updated Terms".[6]
Value Added Resource wrote that because the license is perpetual & irrevocable, removing a listing or closing a shop "may not terminate Etsy's contractual permission to use previously uploaded content", & that Etsy has not clarified how it handles that material in AI training datasets or models.[2]
Objection rights by region
[edit | edit source]
For processing that Etsy bases on its legitimate interests, the Privacy Policy says users in the EEA, the UK & other countries have the right to object to & seek the restriction of that processing.[4] The policy's Right to Object reads:
If we process your information based on our legitimate interests as explained above, or in the public interest, you can object to this processing in certain circumstances. In such cases, we will stop processing your information unless we have compelling legitimate grounds to continue processing or where it is needed for legal reasons.[3]
The policy says users can manage, change, limit, correct or delete their information through their Etsy account settings or profile, & can exercise the listed rights, "subject to applicable law", through the contact options in its Section 12, which include an email address for Etsy's Data Protection Officer.[5] For users located in the United States, the policy says they "may be entitled to additional rights or disclosures" & refers them to a separate United States Regional Privacy Policy.[5]
Value Added Resource wrote that sellers in the European Union & United Kingdom "may have additional rights to object to processing of personal information", though those protections "do not necessarily cover every type of creative content uploaded to the marketplace".[2]
Rules for outside AI tools and agents
[edit | edit source]
Under the heading "Don't Steal Our Stuff", the revised Terms say:
Without limiting the foregoing, you may not use, collect, store, or transmit any content, data, or information obtained from the Services — whether by automated or manual means — for the purpose of developing, training, fine-tuning, evaluating, benchmarking, testing, prompting, distilling, or otherwise contributing to any machine learning model, artificial intelligence system, or related technology, without our express permission.[1]
The Terms marked "Last updated on Sep 30, 2026" already required users to agree not to "crawl, scrape, or spider any page of the Services" without Etsy's "express permission".[6] Value Added Resource reported that Etsy has limited public access to "portions of" its seller community forums, which it said leaves that material harder for outside AI companies to reach while Etsy keeps access for its own technology development.[2]
The revised Terms also treat access to Etsy's services "by automated means", including bots, scripts, browser extensions, artificial intelligence or machine learning systems & "agentic technologies acting on behalf of a user or third party", as use of the Services, & call each suc

report.summary: Etsy's revised terms effective Dec 16, 2026 let Etsy and third-party partners train AI on user uploads, with limited opt-out clarity.
report.background: Etsy is a major online marketplace where sellers upload photos, descriptions, reviews, and community posts. Like many platforms, it is expanding AI features such as listing tools and review summaries, which require large amounts of content. Etsy already held a broad, perpetual license to use seller content for display, translation, promotion, and derivative works. The 2026 update makes AI training an explicit purpose and extends those rights to third-party partners and vendors. The change lands amid growing tension over AI data provenance, creator consent, and regional privacy rules. EU, UK, and EEA users have stronger objection rights, while US sellers face a less clear path. Continued use after notice counts as acceptance, and Etsy tells users who disagree to close their accounts. The revision also restricts outside AI scraping and agentic access, reserving data advantages for Etsy and its partners.
key_points: The revised Terms of Use add explicit permission for Etsy and its third-party partners and vendors to use user content to develop, train, test, and improve AI and machine learning technologies. This covers listing information, reviews, community posts, and other uploads, subject to opt-out rights described in the Privacy Policy.

Etsy's new Privacy Policy says it may use uploaded content to train AI models for features like AI listing tools or AI review summaries. It relies on legitimate interests for this processing, and notes that legal bases may differ for users outside the EEA, Switzerland, and the UK.

Marketplace reporters found no general, clearly named way for US sellers to keep listing photos or descriptions out of AI training while continuing to sell on Etsy. Continued use after notice counts as acceptance, and users who disagree are told they may close their account.

Etsy's existing license is already broad, perpetual, irrevocable, and sub-licensable. Because of that, deleting a listing or closing a shop may not end Etsy's permission to use previously uploaded content, and Etsy has not clarified how that material is handled in AI datasets or models.

The revised terms also ban outside parties from scraping or using Etsy data to train, test, benchmark, or prompt AI systems without express permission. Automated access, including bots, scripts, browser extensions, and agentic technologies, is treated as use of the services.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Etsy's move shows platforms turning user-generated content into a controlled AI asset. It may encourage more explicit AI-training clauses and data-licensing deals, while making unauthorized scraping legally riskier. For developers, the terms raise compliance concerns: building tools that read Etsy listings, reviews, or seller forums could be treated as prohibited AI training or automated access. For sellers and regular users, the practical burden shifts to reading policies, documenting objections, and deciding whether to keep uploading sensitive or valuable creative work. Regional inequality matters: EU and UK users have stronger objection rights, while US sellers may lack a clear opt-out. The broader lesson is that platform terms, not just copyright law, are becoming the front line in AI data governance.
report.tools: To follow or respond, watch Open Terms Archive for tracking terms changes, ToS;DR for plain-language summaries, and Have I Been Trained? for checking whether images appear in public AI datasets. Creators can explore Glaze or Nightshade for image-style protection, though neither guarantees exclusion from training. Sellers should also keep dated records of objections and review Etsy's regional privacy policies.
